prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map places the camera wearer’s torso/lap and forearms nearest, roughly 0.2–0.6 m away, with the hands above the lap at about 0.4–0.7 m; the chairs and floor ahead appear farther away, approximately 1–3 m. It clarifies the foreground-to-background layering: the arms partly occlude the lap, the lap occludes the lower scene, and the central chair stands beyond the small round floor decoration. Across the five frames, the right forearm moves inward and upward toward the left hand while both hands remain within the wearer’s arm’s reach; the larger scene stays at nearly constant depth, indicating little camera translation. Exact metric distances are unreliable because this is monocular depth, and some boundaries around the hands, arms, chair legs, and reflective metal dish are blurred or merged.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map consistently separates the camera wearer’s foreground body from one or two chairs near the upper edge, supporting a layout with the wearer centered below and furniture roughly 1–2 m in front; no separate person is reliably segmented. It makes occlusion boundaries clearer than RGB where the wearer’s hands and arms overlap the torso/lap, and it shows the hands converging near the center-right across the sequence while the chairs remain stationary. Several objects are only partially visible at the image edges, especially the wearer’s body below and furniture above, and most of the floor, cloth, small dish, and hand-held material remain unlabeled. The map is unreliable across frames: the large foreground region is alternately labeled “person” or “bed,” a bright region near the right hand is labeled “knife” despite unstable shape/context, chair instances change or disappear, and mask edges omit substantial parts of the arms and hands.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is entirely black in all five frames, so it provides no body or hand keypoints, facing direction, gaze direction, reach geometry, or motion trajectory. From this map alone, neither the camera wearer’s visible hands nor any other person can be spatially located, and no relative distances or occlusions can be measured. Its complete failure is especially evident because the RGB strip clearly contains two moving hands and forearms within roughly 0.4–0.7 m of the camera. Consequently, every pose-dependent spatial inference—including joint orientation, hand approach across frames, and whether anyone faces or looks toward the camera wearer—is unsupported by this map.
